intro: This branch asks whether adding up infinitely many numbers can give a finite total. It builds a set of tests for deciding when an endless sum settles down.

VI.9.01.what: A sequence is an endless list of numbers. The question is whether the list settles toward one value.

levels.a: Decides whether a sequence settles (converges) or not (diverges).
levels.b: Uses limits of functions to find where a sequence heads.
levels.c: Uses the squeeze idea to trap a sequence.
levels.d: Uses the fact that a list always rising but capped must settle.

VI.9.02.what: A series is the sum of an endless list. It has a total only if the running totals (partial sums) settle down.

levels.a: Computes running totals of a series.
levels.b: Explains that a series has a total when its running totals settle.
levels.c: Sums telescoping series, where most terms cancel out.
levels.d: Writes a series using sigma (summation) notation.

VI.9.03.what: A first check: if the terms don't shrink to zero, the endless sum cannot have a finite total.

levels.a: Explains that terms must shrink to zero for a total to exist.
levels.b: Applies the test to show a series has no total.
levels.c: Explains that shrinking terms alone do not guarantee a total.
levels.d: Uses one plus a half plus a third and so on, which grows forever.

VI.9.04.what: Comparing an endless sum to the area under a curve to decide whether it has a finite total.

levels.a: Checks the conditions needed to use the test.
levels.b: Applies the test to a series.
levels.c: Estimates how much is left over after adding many terms.
levels.d: Links the test to integrals that run out to infinity.

VI.9.05.what: A family of benchmark sums, one over n to a power, whose behavior depends only on that power.

levels.a: Recognizes series of the form one over n to a power.
levels.b: Knows they have a total when the power is bigger than one.
levels.c: Knows the power-one case (the harmonic series) grows forever.
levels.d: Uses these as benchmarks to judge other series.

VI.9.06.what: Deciding about a series by comparing it term by term with one whose behavior is already known.

levels.a: Picks a known series to compare with.
levels.b: Concludes no total when the series is bigger than one that grows forever.
levels.c: Concludes a total exists when it is smaller than one that settles.
levels.d: Writes the full comparison argument clearly.

VI.9.07.what: A more flexible comparison: if two series' terms are roughly in proportion in the long run, they behave the same way.

levels.a: Divides the terms of one series by the other's.
levels.b: Checks that the ratio settles to a positive, finite number.
levels.c: Chooses a good partner series to compare with.

VI.9.08.what: A test for series whose signs flip back and forth, plus and minus.

levels.a: Recognizes a series with alternating signs.
levels.b: Checks that the terms shrink steadily to zero.
levels.c: Concludes the series has a total.
levels.d: Bounds the error when stopping after some terms.

VI.9.09.what: The ratio test compares each term to the one before. If terms shrink by a steady factor below one, the sum is finite.

levels.a: Finds the long-run ratio of each term to the one before.
levels.b: Concludes a total exists when the ratio is less than one.
levels.c: Knows the test gives no answer when the ratio is exactly one.
levels.d: Applies it to series with factorials (products like 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1).

VI.9.10.what: The root test, a cousin of the ratio test, which looks at the nth root of the nth term.

levels.a: Takes the nth root of each term.
levels.b: Applies the test to a series.
levels.c: Recognizes when it is easier than the ratio test.
levels.d: Compares the root and ratio tests.

VI.9.11.what: Some alternating sums settle only because positives and negatives cancel. These behave very differently from sums that settle anyway.

levels.a: Identifies series that settle even with all signs made positive.
levels.b: Identifies series that settle only thanks to the alternating signs.
levels.c: Classifies a series into one of these types.
levels.d: Explores how reordering the second kind can change its total.
